\begin{abstract}
  Urban analysts measure the importance of streets by computing \emph{localised network centrality}: closeness and betweenness scores within distance thresholds. At metropolitan scales these computations become prohibitively expensive, and sampling is the natural remedy. However, when centrality patterns are compared across cities, sampling must be deterministic and network-agnostic; otherwise, different networks would carry different noise levels, making comparison meaningless.

  We present a sampling schedule that depends only on the analysis distance. The key insight is that, under localisation, the relevant population is not the entire network but the neighbourhood reachable within the distance threshold. Adapting the Eppstein--Wang bound to this local setting, and using a canonical grid model to convert distance to neighbourhood size, we obtain a simple formula for the fraction of nodes to sample at each distance. The same sample serves both closeness and betweenness. Validation on the Greater London (\glaNnodes{} nodes) and Greater Madrid (\madridNnodes{} nodes) street networks at 1--20\,km confirms that sampled rankings closely match exact rankings (Spearman $\rho \geq \overallMinRho$). The schedule is implemented in the open-source \cityseer{} Python package \citep{Simons2022}.
\end{abstract}

\textbf{Keywords:} network centrality, sampling, urban morphology, betweenness, harmonic closeness, computational efficiency

%==============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
%==============================================================================

Urban morphological analysis relies on localised network centrality to reveal patterns of accessibility and flow in street networks \citep{Cooper2015}. Two measures are central to this work: \emph{closeness} (how easily a node can reach its neighbours) and \emph{betweenness} (how often a node lies on shortest paths between others). Both are computed within distance thresholds that range from pedestrian ($\approx$500\,m) to metropolitan ($\approx$20\,km) scales, as implemented in tools such as sDNA \citep{Cooper2018} and \cityseer{} \citep{Simons2022}.

Exact computation requires running a shortest-path traversal from every node; the cost scales with both the number of nodes and the size of each node's neighbourhood. A multi-scale analysis of the Greater London network (\glaNnodes{} nodes) across ten distance thresholds takes several hours on a single core. Sampling offers a natural way to reduce this cost: instead of traversing from every node, traverse from a randomly selected fraction and scale up the result.

The challenge is comparability. Each node's centrality is computed over its own local subgraph (the neighbourhood within the distance threshold), and these subgraphs vary in size and density even within a single city. If the sampling rate depended on local structure, nodes in dense areas would carry different noise levels than nodes in sparse areas of the same network, distorting within-city comparisons. The same argument extends to cross-city analysis \citep{Strano2013}: if sampling rates varied by network, results from different cities would not be directly comparable. The schedule must therefore be \emph{deterministic} (the same distance always yields the same sampling probability) and \emph{network-agnostic} (no dependence on local or global network structure). Existing adaptive methods such as KADABRA \citep{Borassi2019} produce network-dependent sample counts, precluding direct comparison.

The key quantity is \emph{reach}: the number of nodes reachable within the distance threshold. At short distances, reach is small and traversals are cheap, so sampling offers little benefit. At long distances, reach is large and each traversal updates many nodes at once, so both the potential speedup and the effective sample size grow with distance.

\citet{Eppstein2004} showed how to bound the required number of samples for global closeness using Hoeffding's concentration inequality. Their bound depends on the total number of nodes in the network. Our approach adapts this bound to the localised setting: under a distance threshold, only the nodes within that threshold matter, so we replace the global node count with the local reach. A canonical grid model then converts distance to reach, making the schedule depend on distance alone. Because each traversal naturally computes both closeness and betweenness, a single schedule serves both metrics.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item A deterministic, network-agnostic sampling schedule for localised closeness and betweenness, where the sampling probability depends only on the analysis distance.
  \item Empirical validation on the Greater London (\glaNnodes{} nodes) and Greater Madrid street networks at 1--20\,km, confirming that sampled rankings closely preserve exact rankings (Spearman $\rho \geq \overallMinRho$) for both metrics.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries} defines the centrality measures. Section~\ref{sec:models} derives the sampling model. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work. Sections~\ref{sec:setup}--\ref{sec:validation} describe the experiments and results. Sections~\ref{sec:discussion} and~\ref{sec:conclusion} discuss practical implications and conclude.

%==============================================================================
\section{Preliminaries}
\label{sec:preliminaries}
%==============================================================================

Both centrality measures are computed with a distance cutoff $d_{\max}$. We write $d$ for $d_{\max}$ when the context is clear.

\paragraph{Harmonic closeness.}
Closeness measures how easily a node can reach its surroundings \citep{Rochat2009, Freeman1979}. For each node $v$, it sums the inverse distances to all nodes within the threshold; nearby nodes contribute more than distant ones:
\begin{equation}
  C_H(v;\, d_{\max}) = \sum_{\substack{u \neq v \\ d(v,u) \leq d_{\max}}} \frac{1}{d(v, u)}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Betweenness.}
Betweenness measures how often a node acts as an intermediary \citep{Freeman1977}. For each node $v$, it counts the fraction of shortest paths (between all other pairs) that pass through $v$:
\begin{equation}
  C_B(v;\, d_{\max}) = \sum_{\substack{s \neq t,\; s \neq v,\; t \neq v \\ d(s,t) \leq d_{\max}}} \frac{\sigma_{st}(v)}{\sigma_{st}}
\end{equation}
where $\sigma_{st}$ is the total number of shortest paths from $s$ to $t$, and $\sigma_{st}(v)$ is the number that pass through $v$. Because shortest paths have optimal substructure, a distance-bounded traversal from each source discovers every node that could contribute to betweenness at that threshold. This property holds for shortest-path (metric) distance; angular (simplest-path) distance \citep{Turner2007} does not satisfy it in general (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).

\paragraph{Reach.}
The \emph{reach} of a node $v$ at threshold $d$ is simply the number of other nodes within distance $d$: $r_v = |\{u : d(v,u) \leq d\}|$. The mean reach across a network, $\bar{r}$, grows with the square of the distance. On a regular grid with inter-node spacing $s = \gridSpacing\,$m, reach follows $r_c = \pi d^2 / s^2$, ranging from about 100 nodes at 1\,km to over 40{,}000 at 20\,km. We call this the \emph{canonical reach} and use it later to build a network-agnostic sampling schedule.

\paragraph{Accuracy metric.}
We evaluate sampling quality using Spearman rank correlation ($\rho$) between sampled and exact centrality values. Urban applications rely on relative rankings (e.g., identifying the most central streets) rather than absolute values, so $\rho$ captures the quantity of practical interest.

%==============================================================================
\section{Sampling Model}
\label{sec:models}
%==============================================================================

\subsection{How many samples are enough?}

The approach follows \citet{Eppstein2004}: select a random subset of nodes as sources, run a distance-bounded shortest-path traversal from each, and scale up the result to estimate what the full computation would have produced (using inverse-probability weighting; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_ht}).

The question is how large the sample needs to be. Hoeffding's inequality \citep{Hoeffding1963} bounds the probability that a sample mean deviates from the true mean by more than a chosen tolerance $\varepsilon$. Applied to closeness estimation for a single target node $v$, it gives:
\[
  \Pr\!\left[\left|\hat{C}_H(v) - C_H(v)\right| > \varepsilon \cdot C_{\max}\right] \leq 2 \exp(-2k\varepsilon^2)
\]
where $k$ is the number of sampled sources that reach $v$, and $C_{\max}$ is the maximum possible contribution from a single source. To guarantee this for all nodes simultaneously, a union bound is applied.

In the global (unbounded) setting of \citet{Eppstein2004}, this union bound runs over all $n$ nodes in the network. Under localisation, however, only the nodes within $d_{\max}$ of $v$ can contribute to $v$'s estimate. This is the key simplification: the relevant population is the local neighbourhood of size $r$ (the reach), not the entire network of size $n$. The union bound therefore runs over $r$ rather than $n$ targets, and the required sample count scales with $\log r$ rather than $\log n$.

Replacing the network-specific reach with the canonical reach $r_c$ (Section~\ref{sec:canonical}) gives the required number of samples and the corresponding sampling probability:
\begin{equation}
  k = \frac{\log(2r_c/\delta)}{2\varepsilon^2}, \qquad
  p = \min\!\left(1,\; \frac{k}{r_c}\right)
  \label{eq:hoeffding_k}
\end{equation}

In words: $p$ is the fraction of nodes to sample at a given distance. It depends on two user-chosen parameters, $\varepsilon$ (error tolerance) and $\delta$ (failure probability), and on the canonical reach $r_c$, which is determined by the analysis distance alone. There are no fitted parameters.

At short distances, the required number of samples exceeds the number of reachable nodes, so $p = 1$ and computation is exact. As distance grows, $p$ decreases and the speedup increases. When a network's actual reach exceeds $r_c$ (as for London; Figure~\ref{fig:val_reach}), the schedule oversamples, strengthening the guarantee. When actual reach falls below $r_c$ (sparse peripheries), the bound is still met because the union bound also shrinks. Empirical results confirm the schedule is conservative across both regimes (Section~\ref{sec:validation}).

\subsection{Shared computation for betweenness}

Each source traversal already explores the local neighbourhood via a bounded Dijkstra. Betweenness can be computed from the same traversal using Brandes' backpropagation algorithm \citep{Brandes2001}, at modest additional cost. The same Hoeffding argument applies: each source's betweenness contribution is bounded, so the same sample count $k$ and probability $p$ (Equation~\ref{eq:hoeffding_k}) suffice for both metrics.

In practice, the bound is more conservative for betweenness than for closeness. Betweenness contributions are heavier-tailed, and the concentration bound ignores the actual (smaller) variance. Betweenness therefore shows tighter margins above the accuracy target than closeness does (Section~\ref{sec:validation}).

\subsection{From reach to distance: the canonical grid model}
\label{sec:canonical}

The sampling probability $p$ depends on reach, which varies not only across networks but across nodes within the same network (dense cores have higher reach than sparse peripheries). To make $p$ depend on distance alone, we substitute a single conservative reference point: the reach of a regular grid with inter-node spacing $s$. On such a grid, the number of nodes within distance $d$ is simply the area of a circle divided by the area per node:
\begin{equation}
  r_c = \frac{\pi d^2}{s^2}
  \label{eq:canonical_reach}
\end{equation}
We set $s = 175$\,m, near the upper end of observed mean block lengths in European street networks (80--180\,m; \citealp{Boeing2017, Strano2013}). This deliberately underestimates the reach of most real neighbourhoods, so the schedule errs on the side of sampling more than strictly necessary. The trade-off is intentional: a small loss of potential speedup buys a single, consistent sampling rate that applies uniformly across all nodes and all networks at a given distance.

Table~\ref{tab:ew_comparison} shows the resulting sampling probabilities at standard analysis distances.

\input{tables/tab1_ew_comparison}

\subsection{Algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
  \caption{Deterministic per-distance sampling for localised network centrality}
  \label{alg:deterministic}
  \begin{algorithmic}[1]
    \Require Network $G = (V, E)$ with live nodes $V_L \subseteq V$ and buffer nodes $V_B = V \setminus V_L$
    \Require Distance thresholds $D = \{d_1, \ldots, d_m\}$
    \Require Error tolerance $\varepsilon$ (default $\hoeffdingEpsilon$), failure probability $\delta$ (default $\hoeffdingDelta$)
    \Require Canonical grid spacing $s$ (default 175\,m)
    \Ensure Closeness estimates $\hat{C}_H[d]$ and betweenness estimates $\hat{C}_B[d]$ for each $d \in D$

    \State $\varphi \gets |V_L| / |V|$ \Comment{Live fraction}
    \For{each distance $d \in D$}
    \State Compute canonical reach: $r_c \gets \pi d^2 / s^2$ \Comment{Eq.~\ref{eq:canonical_reach}}
    \State Compute required sources: $k \gets \ln(2r_c/\delta) / (2\varepsilon^2)$
    \State Compute sampling probability: $p \gets \min(1, k / r_c)$
    \If{$p \geq \varphi$} \Comment{Exact mode is cheaper; Section~\ref{sec:buffer}}
    \State Run exact computation from all sources $s \in V_L$
    \Else
    \State Sample sources $S \subseteq V$ by including each node independently with prob.\ $p$
    \For{each source $s \in S$} \Comment{$S$ includes both live and buffer nodes}
    \State Run distance-bounded Dijkstra from $s$
    \State Accumulate closeness to each live target $v$ via $1/(p \cdot d(s,v))$ \Comment{IPW}
    \State Run Brandes backpropagation; accumulate betweenness for live targets
    \EndFor
    \EndIf
    \EndFor

    \State \Return $\{\hat{C}_H[d],\, \hat{C}_B[d] : d \in D\}$
  \end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

Each distance threshold draws an independent source set. In the implementation, distances where $p \geq \varphi$ (exact mode; see below) are batched so that a single Dijkstra per source serves all such distances simultaneously. Each sampled distance ($p < \varphi$) requires its own pass.

\subsection{Handling boundary effects}
\label{sec:buffer}

Nodes near the edge of a network have artificially low centrality because their neighbourhoods are truncated. The standard remedy \citep{Gil2017} is to surround the study area with a ring of \emph{buffer nodes}: paths can pass through them, but their own centrality values are not reported. Only the interior (\emph{live}) nodes receive results.

In exact mode, only live nodes run as sources, so buffer nodes contribute passively as intermediate steps on paths. Under sampling, the situation is different. Each sampled source contributes to the estimate of every live node it can reach; if buffer nodes are excluded from the source pool, live nodes near the boundary lose contributions from the buffer side, systematically depressing their estimates. We call this \emph{edge roll-off}. To prevent it, buffer nodes must be included in the sampling pool.

This has a cost: the total number of candidate sources is the full network ($n$, including buffer), not just the live nodes ($n_L$). Since exact mode traverses only $n_L$ sources, sampling is faster only when
\begin{equation}
  p < \varphi \equiv \frac{n_L}{n}
  \label{eq:break_even}
\end{equation}
where $\varphi$ is the fraction of live nodes. The effective speedup is $\varphi / p$ rather than $1/p$. When $p \geq \varphi$, the implementation falls back to exact mode, which produces identical (deterministic) results. This fallback is a cost optimisation, not part of the sampling schedule itself: the schedule $p(d)$ remains deterministic and network-agnostic regardless of whether the implementation chooses to use it or to compute exactly. For a network spanning $L$\,km with a buffer of $d_{\max}$\,km on each side, $\varphi \approx (1 - 2d_{\max}/L)^2$.

\subsection{Why the schedule is conservative}
\label{sec:conservatism}

At the default settings ($\varepsilon = \hoeffdingEpsilon$), the schedule is more conservative than it needs to be (Section~\ref{sec:validation}). Three factors contribute. First, the Hoeffding bound uses only the range of contributions and ignores the actual (much smaller) variance. Second, the union bound treats node-level errors as independent, even though they are positively correlated. Third, the accuracy metric (Spearman $\rho$) measures rank preservation, which is more forgiving than additive error: small absolute errors rarely change the ordering among well-separated nodes, and the highest-centrality nodes have the largest neighbourhoods and therefore the most precise estimates.

\label{sec:related}

  \label{tab:bounds_comparison}

    \midrule
    \multicolumn{5}{@{}l}{\emph{Source-sampling (full traversal per sample)}} \\[2pt]
    Eppstein \& Wang \citeyearpar{Eppstein2004} & Closeness & Additive, global & $O(\log n / \varepsilon^2)$ & $n$ \\
    Brandes \& Pich \citeyearpar{Brandes2007} & Both & Empirical & User-chosen & --- \\
    Bader et al.\ \citeyearpar{Bader2007} & Betw. & Relative, per vertex & $O(1 / (\varepsilon^2 b(v)))$ & $b(v)$ \\

    \multicolumn{5}{@{}l}{\emph{Path-sampling (single shortest path per sample)}} \\[2pt]
    Riondato et al.\ \citeyearpar{Riondato2016} & Betw. & Additive, global & $O(\log \text{VD} / \varepsilon^2)$ & VD \\
    KADABRA \citeyearpar{Borassi2019} & Betw. & Additive, global & Adaptive & $D$ \\
    SILVAN \citeyearpar{Pellegrina2023} & Betw. & Non-uniform & Variance-dep. & Variance \\[4pt]
    \midrule
    \textbf{This work} & \textbf{Both} & \textbf{Additive, local\textsuperscript{*}} & $\boldsymbol{O(\log r / \varepsilon^2)}$ & $\boldsymbol{r}$ \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}

  \vspace{0.3em}
  \footnotesize \textsuperscript{*}Union bound over the $r$ nodes within each distance neighbourhood, not over all $n$ nodes globally (Section~\ref{sec:models}).
\end{table}

\emph{Source-sampling} selects a subset of nodes and traverses the network from each. \citet{Brandes2007} established this approach empirically for both closeness and betweenness. \citet{Geisberger2008} refined betweenness estimation with distance-weighted corrections. \citet{Bader2007} used adaptive sampling with per-vertex guarantees. None of these methods provides a deterministic, distance-based schedule suitable for comparative multi-scale analysis.

\emph{Path-sampling} \citep{Riondato2016, Borassi2019, Pellegrina2023} draws random source--target pairs and computes one shortest path per sample. It does not adapt easily to localised analysis: the set of admissible pairs depends on local morphology, each sample updates only one path (whereas a single source traversal updates all reachable nodes), and path-sampling applies only to betweenness. Our approach uses source-sampling, which naturally serves both metrics from the same traversals.

%==============================================================================
\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}
%==============================================================================

\paragraph{Synthetic networks.}
We generate synthetic networks using \nTopologies{} topology templates: trellis (regular grid with diagonal connections; average degree $\approx 4$), tree (hierarchical branching; average degree $\approx 2.3$), and linear (constrained grid; average degree $\approx 3$). These span the range from highly connected planned cores (trellis) to low-connectivity suburban development (tree). Each topology is tiled to create networks of approximately 12\,km extent; accuracy is evaluated on a central 4\,km$\times$4\,km window to reduce edge effects. We test \nDistances{} distance thresholds from 500\,m to \syntheticMaxDist{}\,m and \nEpsilons{} error tolerances from $\varepsilon = 0.02$ to $0.1$.

\paragraph{Boundary effects.}
Nodes near network edges have artificially low centrality because their surroundings are truncated. Following standard practice \citep{Gil2017}, we surround the study area with a ring of buffer nodes equal in depth to the maximum analysis distance. Only interior (\emph{live}) nodes receive centrality values; the buffer nodes participate in path computations but are not reported. Under sampling, buffer nodes must also serve as potential sources to avoid edge roll-off (Section~\ref{sec:buffer}).

\paragraph{Validation networks.}
We validate on two real-world street networks: the Greater London Authority (GLA) road network (Ordnance Survey Open Roads; \glaNnodes{} nodes after preprocessing) and the Greater Madrid metropolitan network (\madridNnodes{} nodes). Both networks use a \glaBuffer{}\,km inward buffer. We report the mean over three random seeds; inter-seed variation in $\rho$ is small (standard deviation $< 0.002$ at all distances). Ground truth uses all sources ($p = 1.0$) and is deterministic.

%==============================================================================
\section{Validation}
\label{sec:validation}
%==============================================================================

\subsection{Synthetic networks}

Figure~\ref{fig:headline} shows how ranking accuracy varies with error tolerance across the synthetic topologies. The tree topology, which has the most heterogeneous centrality distribution, comfortably exceeds $\rho = \targetRho$ for both closeness and betweenness. The linear and trellis topologies fall below the target at $\varepsilon = \hoeffdingEpsilon$, for different reasons.

The trellis is a regular grid where over 90\% of nodes share the same betweenness value (signal-to-noise ratio $\approx 2$). Spearman $\rho$ is effectively meaningless here: there is no meaningful rank ordering to preserve, and even tiny sampling noise produces random permutations among tied nodes. The absolute errors remain small; it is the metric ($\rho$) that breaks down, not the estimator.

The linear topology has a compressed closeness distribution (coefficient of variation $\approx 0.05$; signal-to-noise ratio $\approx 8$). Sampling noise is small in absolute terms but comparable to the narrow spread of true values, so $\rho$ is depressed.

These results reflect a fundamental limitation of rank-based evaluation on near-uniform distributions, not a deficiency of the schedule. Real street networks have far more heterogeneous centrality distributions: the Greater London and Greater Madrid networks both achieve $\rho > \targetRho$ at all distances (Section~\ref{sec:validation}), with signal-to-noise ratios exceeding 50.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_rho_vs_epsilon.pdf}
  \caption{Ranking accuracy (Spearman $\rho$) vs.\ error tolerance $\varepsilon$ for closeness (A) and betweenness (B), across synthetic topologies and distances. Per-topology lines are shown alongside the bold mean. The green dashed line marks $\rho = \targetRho$; the grey dotted line marks the default $\varepsilon = \hoeffdingEpsilon$. The trellis topology falls below the threshold because its regular grid produces many near-identical centrality values, making rank ordering sensitive to small perturbations.}
  \label{fig:headline}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Real-world validation}

Tables~\ref{tab:validation} and~\ref{tab:madrid_validation} report results for Greater London and Greater Madrid respectively. Both networks achieve $\rho > \targetRho$ for closeness and betweenness at all distances from 1--20\,km. Betweenness at 20\,km is the limiting case: $\rho = \glaMinRhoBetweenness$ (London) and $\rho = \madridMinRhoBetweenness$ (Madrid).

\input{tables/tab2_validation}

\input{tables/tab4_madrid_validation}

At short distances the required sample fraction is high enough that exact computation is cheaper, so the implementation uses exact mode automatically (Section~\ref{sec:buffer}). Speedup emerges at longer distances, where only a small fraction of nodes need to be sampled.

The two networks represent different ends of the European urban spectrum (Figure~\ref{fig:val_accuracy}). London is denser, with actual reach consistently above the canonical model (Figure~\ref{fig:val_reach}), so the schedule samples more than strictly necessary and accuracy margins are wide. Madrid's sparser outskirts bring actual reach closer to the canonical estimate, providing a harder test of the bound's built-in conservatism.

\subsection{Error structure}

Absolute errors grow with reach, but \emph{relative} errors shrink (Figure~\ref{fig:error_crossover}): the most important nodes (those with the highest centrality and largest neighbourhoods) are estimated most precisely. Errors are spatially uniform, with no systematic bias in dense cores or sparse peripheries (Figure~\ref{fig:spatial_error}). Most nodes remain in the same centrality decile under sampling, with the strongest stability in the upper deciles (Figure~\ref{fig:decile_transition}).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering

  \caption{Per-node median errors pooled across reach quartiles at distances where $p < 1$, for Greater London (circles) and Greater Madrid (squares). (A) Absolute error increases with reach. (B) Relative error decreases with reach: precision scales with centrality importance.}
  \label{fig:error_crossover}
\end{figure}

%==============================================================================
\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
%==============================================================================

\subsection{Practical guidance}

In \cityseer{}, the user sets a single parameter ($\varepsilon$, the error tolerance) and the library automatically determines how much to sample at each distance. Algorithm~\ref{alg:deterministic} gives the full procedure for manual implementations. Table~\ref{tab:distance_lookup} and Figure~\ref{fig:guide} show the schedule at standard distances.

\input{tables/tab_distance_lookup}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig3_practical_guide.pdf}
  \caption{(A) Sampling probability $p$ vs.\ analysis distance at default settings. (B) Theoretical speedup $1/p$. These values assume no boundary buffer; on buffered networks, the implementation falls back to exact mode when $p \geq \varphi$ (Section~\ref{sec:buffer}), so sampling only engages at longer distances.}
  \label{fig:guide}
\end{figure}

Table~\ref{tab:distance_lookup} and Figure~\ref{fig:guide} show the sampling probability and theoretical speedup ($1/p$) as a function of distance alone. In practice, networks analysed with a boundary buffer have a live fraction $\varphi < 1$ (Section~\ref{sec:buffer}), and the implementation falls back to exact computation at any distance where $p \geq \varphi$. For example, at $\varepsilon = \hoeffdingEpsilon$, the schedule prescribes $p \approx 59\%$ at 5\,km, but if the live fraction is $\varphi = 0.50$ (as for Greater London), exact mode is cheaper and sampling does not engage. At 10\,km ($p \approx 17\%$) and 20\,km ($p \approx 5\%$), sampling is active and the realised speedup is $\varphi / p$ rather than $1/p$. Larger networks have higher $\varphi$ and benefit more; analyses where the buffer zone is large relative to the study area see less benefit.

Halving $\varepsilon$ quadruples the number of required samples. A tighter tolerance ($\varepsilon = 0.04$) is recommended for grid-like networks (where many nodes have near-identical centrality) but roughly halves the speedup. A looser tolerance ($\varepsilon = 0.1$) still yields $\rho > 0.99$ on synthetic networks and is suitable for exploratory work.

Betweenness is the limiting factor: it requires more samples than closeness at the same tolerance. Users computing only closeness can safely use a looser tolerance ($\varepsilon = 0.08$--$0.1$).

For small networks (under about 1{,}000 nodes), exact computation completes in seconds and sampling is unnecessary. For unfamiliar network types, a pilot comparison at one long distance (e.g., 10\,km) can verify that $\rho > \targetRho$ before committing to the schedule.

\subsection{What the guarantee does and does not cover}

The Hoeffding bound guarantees that absolute errors stay within a tolerance. Our validation measures something different: whether the \emph{ranking} of nodes is preserved (Spearman $\rho$). No formal bound connects the two. The empirical success rests on a structural property of street networks: centrality values are spread across several orders of magnitude, so small additive errors rarely change the ordering among well-separated nodes. The bound provides the mathematical form of the schedule; the ranking accuracy is a validated empirical outcome, not a formal guarantee.

\subsection{Scope and limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

The schedule applies to shortest-path (metric) distance only. Angular distance (simplest-path) \citep{Turner2007} does not satisfy the subpath optimality assumed in the betweenness derivation and remains to be tested. Validation covers two European cities; networks with very different structure (e.g., North American grids) may benefit from a tighter tolerance ($\varepsilon = 0.04$) or a pilot comparison.

The canonical grid model substitutes a fixed spacing for the actual network structure: denser networks are oversampled, while sparser networks rely on the built-in conservatism of the bound (Figure~\ref{fig:val_reach}). The effective speedup also depends on the live fraction $\varphi$, which shrinks as the buffer grows relative to the study area, so analyses with large distance thresholds on small networks see less benefit.

\subsection{Future work}

Extending validation to angular distance and to a broader range of global morphologies are natural next steps. Adaptive per-node sampling, online stopping criteria \citep{Borassi2019}, and variance-aware bounds \citep{Pellegrina2023} could further improve efficiency.

%==============================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
%==============================================================================

We have presented a sampling schedule for localised network centrality that depends only on the analysis distance. The core idea is to replace the global network size in existing concentration bounds with the local neighbourhood size (reach), and to use a canonical grid model so that the schedule requires no per-network calibration. The same sample serves both closeness and betweenness. Boundary buffer nodes must be included in the source pool to prevent edge effects, which reduces the effective speedup but preserves accuracy. Validation on the Greater London and Greater Madrid street networks at distances from 1 to 20\,km confirms that sampled rankings closely match exact rankings ($\rho \geq \overallMinRho$), with errors distributed uniformly across the network.

The schedule is implemented in the open-source \cityseer{} Python package.\footnote{\href{https://github.com/benchmark-urbanism/cityseer-api}{github.com/benchmark-urbanism/cityseer-api}} Analysis scripts and validation data are available in the repository's \texttt{analysis/sampling/} directory.

\section{Technical Details}

\paragraph{Synthetic network generation.}

Synthetic networks are generated using tile-based templates. Each template defines a connectivity pattern within a single tile; tiles are then arrayed to create networks of the desired extent.

\begin{description}
  \item[Trellis] A regular grid with diagonal connections, representing highly connected urban cores. Average degree $\approx 4$.

  \item[Tree] A hierarchical branching structure where each node connects to at most 3 others. Represents suburban cul-de-sac development. Average degree $\approx 2.3$.

  \item[Linear] A constrained grid with fewer cross-connections than trellis. Intermediate connectivity. Average degree $\approx 3$.
\end{description}

Networks are tiled 24$\times$24 to achieve approximately 12\,km extent, then the largest connected component is extracted. Node positions are perturbed slightly to avoid perfectly regular spacing.

\paragraph{GLA network preprocessing.}

The Greater London Authority road network is sourced from Ordnance Survey Open Roads data (GeoPackage format).

Preprocessing steps:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Remove invalid and empty geometries
  \item Explode multi-part geometries
  \item Build NetworkX graph from edges
  \item Remove filler nodes (degree-2 nodes that do not represent junctions)
  \item Remove dangling nodes (dead-end segments $< 20\,$m)
  \item Consolidate nearby nodes (threshold 1\,m)
  \item Extract largest connected component
\end{enumerate}

Final network: \glaNnodes{} nodes.

\paragraph{Madrid network.}

The Greater Madrid metropolitan network (\madridNnodes{} nodes) is sourced from OpenStreetMap via the OSMnx library \citep{Boeing2017} and preprocessed using the same consolidation pipeline as the GLA network.

\paragraph{Correctness verification.}

We verified the Rust-based \cityseer{} implementation against NetworkX \citep{Hagberg2008} across all three synthetic topologies, distance thresholds from 200\,m to 3200\,m, both distance heuristics, and both metrics. The maximum per-node difference was below $10^{-6}$ in all configurations, attributable to floating-point precision.

\paragraph{Inverse-probability weighting.}
\label{sec:appendix_ht}

When only a fraction $p$ of nodes are sampled as sources, each sampled contribution is scaled by $1/p$ to estimate what the full computation would have produced. This is a standard Horvitz--Thompson estimator \citep{Horvitz1952} and is unbiased whenever $p > 0$. The source pool includes both live and buffer nodes (Section~\ref{sec:buffer}), ensuring that every node which contributes in exact mode has a chance of being sampled.

For closeness, each source's contribution to a target depends only on the distance between them, so contributions from different sources are independent. For betweenness, the Brandes decomposition likewise yields independent per-source terms, so the same argument applies.

\paragraph{Betweenness pair-weighting under sampling.}

When buffer nodes are included as sources, pairs where both endpoints are buffer nodes are excluded (these contribute no betweenness in exact mode either). When both endpoints can run as sources, each direction contributes half the credit to avoid double-counting. When only one direction runs (live source to buffer target), the full credit is assigned in that direction.

\paragraph{Implementation in \cityseer{}.}

The sampling model is implemented in the \cityseer{} Python package (version 4.25+). Sampling is enabled via the \texttt{sample=True} flag. When enabled, the library automatically computes the live fraction $\varphi$ and falls back to exact mode at distances where $p \geq \varphi$ (Section~\ref{sec:buffer}). The \texttt{node\_centrality\_shortest} function computes both closeness and betweenness from shared Dijkstra traversals in a single call:

\begin{verbatim}
from cityseer.metrics import networks

gdf = networks.centrality_shortest(
    network_structure,
    nodes_gdf,
    distances=[500,1000,2000,5000,10000,20000],
    sample=True
)
\end{verbatim}

Convenience wrappers (\texttt{closeness\_shortest}, \texttt{betweenness\_shortest}) are available for computing a single metric, but using them separately forgoes the shared-traversal advantage.

The default error tolerance ($\varepsilon = \hoeffdingEpsilon$) and failure probability ($\delta = \hoeffdingDelta$) are set in \texttt{cityseer.config}. The \texttt{cityseer.sampling} module provides helper functions for custom workflows:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \texttt{compute\_distance\_p}: deterministic $p$ from distance via canonical grid model (recommended entry point)
  \item \texttt{compute\_hoeffding\_p}: Hoeffding bound from a given reach value (for experimentation with non-canonical schedules)
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Reproducibility.}

All analysis scripts and validation results are available at \href{https://github.com/benchmark-urbanism/cityseer-api/tree/master/analysis/sampling}{analysis/sampling/}. The current script pipeline runs sequentially from \texttt{00\_generate\_cache.py} through \texttt{05\_generate\_macros.py} via \texttt{run\_all.py}, with each script's outputs documented in its header.
